CA-05.001: anatomy describes the structure of bodies. physiology describes how those structures work. a bone, muscle and tendon can be examined as objects and also studied together to explain how a person moves a joint. human tissues contain cells organized for different roles. tissues form organs such as the heart, and organs cooperate in systems. a structure can serve several systems. for example, the tongue helps move food, bears structures involved in taste, and participates in speech. a teaching model shows selected structures at one level of detail. people differ in their anatomy, development, abilities and lived experience. anatomy physiology
CA-05.002: development includes changes in the structure and function of the body over time. early in development, repeated cell division produces groups of cells. cells differentiate as they take on distinct roles, such as contributing to muscle or nervous tissue. inherited variants help shape biological development together with conditions before and after birth. during growth and aging, bodies change at different rates. for example, inherited differences and lived conditions can contribute to differences in mobility in later life. a life-stage sequence is a simplified description of development. it cannot predict an individual's health, milestones or experience. development differentiation
CA-05.003: cognition describes processes such as attending to information, remembering, learning and solving problems. seeing an object uses sensory signals. recognizing it can also depend on prior experience. cognitive abilities and experiences vary within a person over time and across people. a language gives a community shared ways to combine meaningful expressions. speech uses sounds. signed languages use movements and spatial relationships of hands, face and body. a writing system uses visible or tactile marks to record parts of language. the sign-language photograph documents a specific exchange and does not define what the signs mean. there is no one-to-one mapping across all languages and experiences. the archive's language bridge supplies examples whose interpretations need testing. cognition writing system
CA-05.004: the human body can be described at several scales. molecules form cellular structures; cells cooperate within tissues; tissues form organs; and organs work together in systems. these levels describe relationships within a single living organism. the heart, blood and blood vessels form a transport system. the respiratory system exchanges gases with the surroundings, while muscles and skeletal structures enable movement. other systems coordinate responses, process nutrients and maintain internal conditions. their functions overlap: no organ system is completely independent of the rest of the body. the model describes general human biology; individuals differ in anatomy, development and function. tissue organ
CA-05.005: bones support the body, protect some organs and provide surfaces on which muscles can act. a joint is where bones meet. some joints allow a large range of motion, while others allow very little. tendons transmit force from muscles to bones. at the elbow, muscle force can bend or straighten the arm. skeletal muscle can shorten as its fibers generate tension. motion usually involves several muscles and coordinated signals from the nervous system. the pottery photograph shows one activity in which the hand's joints, muscles and sense of touch work together. an articulated museum skeleton shows the arrangement of bones. it omits living tissue and some features that vary with age, development, disability and individual anatomy. tendon joint
CA-05.006: the heart pumps blood through two connected circuits. the right side sends blood to the lungs. blood returning from the lungs enters the left side, which pumps it through vessels to the rest of the body. small vessels called capillaries exchange materials with surrounding tissues. air enters the lungs during inhalation. at small air sacs called alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into air that can be exhaled. the blood transports oxygen to tissues and carries carbon dioxide away. breathing and cellular respiration describe different processes. the diagram shows the flow of blood after birth at a simplified scale. the fetal circulation uses different pathways, and real blood vessels form branching networks. pulmonary circulation alveolus
CA-05.007: digestion changes food into forms the body can use. teeth break food into smaller pieces. in the stomach and intestines, movement mixes the contents with fluids, and enzymes split many large molecules. the liver makes bile, which helps process fats, and the pancreas supplies several digestive enzymes. much of the absorption of nutrients takes place across the wall of the small intestine. the large intestine absorbs water, and its microorganisms transform some compounds that reach it. circulation distributes absorbed materials to tissues. food and meals vary across communities and individuals. these descriptions explain physiology without specifying a diet or treating one daily practice as universal. digestion absorption
CA-05.008: the brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. nerves connect it to much of the body. neurons convey signals through changes in electrical activity and often communicate with other cells using chemical signals. these networks support movement, coordination and the processing of information. receptor cells respond to particular kinds of input. cells in the retina respond to light. vibrations transmitted through the ear can move sensory cells in the inner ear and produce signals. other receptors respond to mechanical force, chemicals or temperature. signals from many receptors are combined during perception. the eye photograph shows an external part of the eye. the ear record depicts a model and the microscopy record shows rat neurons. human sensory experience and abilities vary. neuron sensory receptor
CA-05.009: homeostasis describes regulated conditions in the body, such as temperature, staying within ranges compatible with function. when body temperature rises, evaporation of sweat can remove heat. this is a feedback process because the response changes the condition that helped trigger it. several systems help protect tissue from damage and infection. skin and other barriers restrict entry. immune cells can respond to signs of damage or foreign material; some mount more targeted responses. antibodies can bind specific targets, and some immune cells persist after a response, supporting a faster response on later encounters. normal ranges and responses vary across people and circumstances. these examples describe basic physiology, and immune activity can also damage healthy tissue. homeostasis antibody
CA-05.010: in sexual reproduction, fertilization joins an egg and sperm, forming a cell called a zygote. as cells divide, groups specialize into tissues. during development in the uterus, the placenta supports exchanges of materials between the pregnant individual and the developing organism. ultrasound imaging uses echoes to show some structures before birth. human bodies continue to change after birth. genes, environments and lived conditions influence development and aging. individual variation includes differences in body proportions, sensory abilities and rates of change. images of people at different life stages can show examples of variation. life stages are descriptive and can be defined differently by culture and purpose. a single ultrasound and a single group portrait show individuals at particular times. fertilization placenta
